Datasets For exact length control, we utilize the CNN/DailyMail dataset (CNNDM, Nallapati et al. (2016)), where the length instruction $\ell$ is extracted from the references. For length-interval control, we use the Alpaca-Eval-LI (ALPACA) and MT-BenchLI (MTBENCH) datasets (Yuan et al., 2024), which are derived from the Alpaca-Eval dataset (Dubois et al., 2024b) and the MT-Bench dataset (Zheng et al., 2023). The length interval instructions are already provided in the dataset, where $\ell_1 = 0$ and $\ell_2$ is the length of the reference response. For CNNDM, we randomly choose 1000 samples from the 3.0 version of the test set, since the instruction following task contains 1042 samples (802 from ALPACA and 240 from MTBENCH). LLMs We evaluate the effectiveness of our framework in the latest LLMs, including Llama-2-7B (LLAMA2, Touvron et al. (2023b), Qwen-2.5-7B (QWEN2.5, Team (2024)), Llama-3/3.1-8B (LLAMA3/3.1, Dubey et al. (2024)), and GPT-3.5/4 (Achiam et al., 2023). For white-box LLMs like LLAMA, we use them as black-box models, where the maximum iteration trial is 5 with a beam size of 16. Our experiments are implemented on the Huggingface Transformers package1. All LLMs we used are the chat version trained with supervised fine tuning, where LLAMA2 and QWEN2.5 have 7B parameters while LLAMA3 and LLAMA3.1 have 8B parameters. The generation configurations of each model are set by default, as demonstrated in Table 9. There is no training stage of our framework, and the inference is performed on an NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU with a random seed of 0. For the CNN/Daily Mail dataset, we randomly choose 1000 samples from the 3.0 version of the test set, since the instruction following task contains 1042 samples (802 from Alpaca-Eval-LI and 240 from MT-Bench-LI). We conduct a human evaluation involving three Ph.D. students with expertise in natural language processing and IELTS scores of at least 6.5. Each evaluator is presented with the article and the paired summaries of two methods (OURS and INST). They are tasked with assigning a score for each pair as a win, tie, or lose based on the informativeness and conciseness of each summary. We randomly shuffle the demonstrated position of summaries from different samplers and the evaluators are blinded to the identity of the samplers to prevent bias. We randomly select 100 cases for each model on CNNDM. To compensate for the inability to hire native English-speaking evaluators, we further leverage state-of-the-art English-oriented LLMs as additional evaluators, which are GPT-4o-latest, MetaLlama-3.1-405B-Instruct, and claude-3.5-sonnet20241022. These models have been extensively validated in numerous studies, demonstrating per Table 11: Human Evaluation: Ours vs INST. (three LLM evaluators)
ModelsWIN↑TIELOSE↓KAPPA↑

LLAMA3.156.0%11.0%33.0%0.59

ModelsWIN↑TIELOSE↓KAPPA↑

LLAMA3.159.0%12.5%30.5%0.48
formance that exceeds human evaluators in various NLP tasks. By incorporating both human and AI-based assessments, we ensure a more comprehensive and reliable evaluation of summary quality. The results and kappa correlations among three human evaluators, three LLM evaluators, and three human and three LLM evaluators are demonstrated in Tables 10 to 12. We can observe that the human evaluations are highly aligned with the LLM annotations, with strong kappa correlations. Our method shows a significant advantage over the instruction baseline considering the informativeness and conciseness of the summaries. This improvement is not in line with the ROUGE score. Because the ROUGE score calculates the correlation between the generated summaries and the reference summaries, and the zero-shot / one-shot LLMs share a totally different distribution compared to the references. Therefore, our method can improve both the accuracy of length control and the quality of generated contents. In addition, the slight decrease in the ROUGE score of our method can be explained by the fact that ROUGE is a recall score and it is easy for longer contents to have a higher score.
